citation.title: Real-time multi-objective topology optimization method via deep learning
citation.authors: Cheng Xiang; Airong Chen; Dalei Wang; Rujin Ma
citation.venue: Bridge Maintenance, Safety, Management, Digitalization and Sustainability (IABMAS 2024 proceedings, CRC Press/Taylor & Francis), book chapter
citation.version_coded: Open-access edition PDF (CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, per the chapter's own header), downloaded from the publisher's own file host (Taylor & Francis's oa-edit API, which redirected to an Amazon S3 URL under taylorfrancis.com's content store) and read in full (8 pp.) with PyMuPDF text extraction. Only version; no arXiv preprint exists.

claim.primary_outcome_paraphrase: On a 40x80 cantilever test set, the trained SWPUnet (a UNet with Swin-style shifted-window attention in its skip connections) predicts a near-optimal multi-objective (compliance/stress/volume) structure in 0.0076 s on average, versus 15.76 s for the conventional MMA-based iterative method, a time saving the article reports as 99.97%, with average compliance, stress and volume errors of -7.50%, -5.08% and 0.84%.
claim.location: Section 4 (main text; the Abstract and Conclusion state the efficiency gain only qualitatively -- e.g. 'a significant reduction in computation cost ... with little sacrifice on the performance of design solutions' -- with no numbers, and the Introduction gives no comparison numbers of its own)
claim.claimed_speedup_basis: Derived as classical time / ML time = 15.76 s / 0.0076 s ≈ 2073.7 [derived] from the two headline averages in Sec. 4 and Table 1. The article's own percentage statements in the same paragraph are internally inconsistent and are reported here rather than adopted: 'only 0.026% of traditional methods' would imply an ML time of about 0.0041 s (not the stated 0.0076 s), and 'efficiency improved by 99.97%' (matching Table 1's 'Time saved: 99.97%') implies a ratio of about 3,333x -- neither matches the 2,073.7x obtained directly from the two printed times [observed inconsistency in the source, not resolved by the coder]. The ML time (0.0076 s = ~9.4×10⁻⁴ s preprocessing + ~4.42×10⁻³ s prediction, Sec. 4) explicitly excludes dataset-generation and training time ('the considerable time of generating the dataset and training the neural network are not included').
claim.alternatives: None distinct from the primary outcome: Table 1 (Ec -7.50%, EσPN -5.08%, Ev 0.84%, Epix 5.18%, outperform-rate 49.75%, large-error-rate 5.90%, time saved 99.97%) is the article's single, comprehensive speed-and-quality comparison, and every number cited above is drawn from it or its surrounding paragraph in Sec. 4.

baseline.classical_method: Method of Moving Asymptotes (MMA, Svanberg 1987), gradient-based nonlinear TO minimizing compliance subject to a volume constraint and a p-norm (p=6) aggregated von Mises stress constraint, SIMP-type density interpolation (Sec. 2, Eq. 1)
baseline.implementation: not stated (no software, library, or code source named for the MMA/FE baseline)
baseline.hardware_classical: not stated anywhere in the article
baseline.hardware_ml: not stated anywhere in the article
baseline.problem_size: 2D cantilever beam, 40x80 element resolution (41x81-node input tensor), volume fraction 0.3-0.7, stress fraction 0.0-1.0 (Sec. 3.1)
baseline.classical_iterations: not stated precisely; described only as 'hundreds of iterations of finite element analysis and sensitivity analysis' (Sec. 4)
baseline.ml_time: 0.0076 s average, decomposed as ~9.4×10⁻⁴ s data preprocessing + ~4.42×10⁻³ s model prediction (Sec. 4) [these two components sum to ≈5.36×10⁻³ s, not exactly the stated 0.0076 s; reported as printed]
baseline.training_time: not stated (136 training epochs run, validation loss minimised at epoch 116, Sec. 3.3, but no wall-clock time given)
baseline.data_generation_cost: not stated; 20,000 MMA-optimized samples were generated (train:val:test = 8:1:1, Sec. 3.1) but no compute time or cost is reported, and the article explicitly says this cost is excluded from the headline speed-up (Sec. 4)
baseline.quality_metric: Compliance error (Ec), p-norm stress error (EσPN), volume-fraction error (Ev), and pixel-accuracy error (Epix), each comparing the predicted structure to the MMA/FE result for the same case; the article also reports von Mises stress distributions of the predicted structures (Fig. 4a), consistent with an FE-based (not purely image-based) evaluation of stress and compliance, though the article never states in so many words that it re-runs FE analysis on the predicted density field [inferred from context]
baseline.quality_gap: Table 1 averages: Ec -7.50%, EσPN -5.08%, Ev 0.84%, Epix 5.18%; outperform-rate (predicted result at least as good as MMA on all three of Ev/Ec/EσPN) 49.75%; large-error rate (Ec or EσPN beyond 20%) 5.90%, attributed to high stress sensitivity to topology changes and to disconnected structures in some DL predictions (Sec. 4)

R1.evidence: Sec. 4, Table 1: the 2,073.7x-derived speed claim is reported alongside a full quality accounting on the same test set -- matched volume fraction (Ev 0.84% average error), compliance and stress within single-digit average error (Ec -7.50%, EσPN -5.08%, both negative, i.e. the ML result is on average slightly stiffer/lower-stress than the classical one), and an explicit large-error rate (5.90%) rather than a single cherry-picked example. Close to half the test set (outperform-rate 49.75%) meets the article's own 'as good or better' bar. This is not a speed claim made with no quality comparison, and quality is not measurably and systematically worse outside a stated error band.

R2.evidence: No hardware of any kind (CPU/GPU model, core count) is stated for either the classical MMA/FE baseline or the neural network, so hardware comparability cannot be assessed (matches the protocol's partial condition 'the hardware choice is not justified' -- here it is not even disclosed). The problem is very small (40x80 elements, on the order of 3x10³ design variables), well below the 10⁵-DOF threshold for R2(c), so a GPU-vs-CPU-at-scale concern does not arise regardless. No solver type is named for the FE step inside MMA, and the classical iteration count is given only as 'hundreds', not a precise number, so R2(d) cannot be established from the text and R2(a)/(e) would need a re-test or an explicit per-iteration time, neither available here.

R3.evidence: Sec. 4 explicitly states: 'It should be noted that the considerable time of generating the dataset and training the neural network are not included' in the 0.0076 s / 99.97% figure. This is an explicit statement limiting the speed claim to per-query inference (data preprocessing + model prediction only), which the protocol's R3 pass condition accepts in place of a full data-generation-plus-training cost accounting with break-even.

R4.evidence: Quality is judged primarily by physically meaningful FE-linked quantities -- compliance error, p-norm stress error and volume-fraction error, plus an explicit comparison of predicted vs. classical von Mises stress fields (Fig. 4a) -- not solely by the image-similarity metric present (pixel-accuracy error, Epix, one of four reported metrics). Failure is quantified: a large-error rate of 5.90% (Ec or EσPN beyond 20%) is reported and its causes (stress sensitivity to topology, disconnected structures in some DL outputs) are discussed with an example (Fig. 4b). The article does not explicitly state that it re-runs an independent FE analysis on the returned (possibly rounded) density field, which is noted as an inference rather than a confirmed fact.

notes: Short (8-page) open-access conference-proceedings chapter (IABMAS 2024 / CRC Press), read in full; no supplementary material found or expected for this format. included.method_family='cnn': SWPUnet is explicitly 'a novel extension of Unet' (Sec. 3.2) with Swin-Transformer-style shifted-window self-attention (SWA) added only within the skip connections; the backbone is a CNN encoder-decoder, so 'cnn' was chosen over 'transformer'. included.physics='compliance' because Eq. 1 minimizes compliance subject to volume and (p-norm) stress constraints -- stress is a constraint here, not the optimization objective. A clear internal numerical inconsistency in the article's own headline speed-up statement is flagged in claim.claimed_speedup_basis rather than silently resolved. Two same-group prior papers are cited as background/related work (Wang et al. 2021, Engineering Optimization; Xiang et al. 2022 x2, Thin-Walled Structures and Structural and Multidisciplinary Optimization) but are single-objective (compliance- or stress-only) predecessors, not duplicates of this multi-objective chapter; none of the three appears in audit/pool/pool.csv under a matching title, and this chapter's own title/DOI has no other pool match. No author named Jun Wang (authors: Cheng Xiang, Airong Chen, Dalei Wang, Rujin Ma; a cited related-work author is D. Wang, a different person from a different paper).
